newsitem.title: UK: New UK regulation won't stop derivatives dramas.
newsitem.headline: New UK regulation won't stop derivatives dramas.

text.p: Sweeping changes to financial regulation in Britain are unlikely to put an end to derivatives' debacles like the one which hit Barings, but they should help polish the industry's tarnished image, experts said on Wednesday.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown unveiled plans on Tuesday to transfer responsibility for supervising banks from the Bank of England (BOE) to a strengthened Securities and Investment Board. The new SIB will also regulate securities firms and insurance companies.
"Under the old system you could say there were too many
chefs in the kitchen," said Anthony Belchambers, chief executive of the Futures and Options Association. "But on the other hand, perhaps London is too big a kitchen for one chef."
Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs), the so-called
front-line regulators, will be wrapped into the new SIB.
Analysts said they need the details of what kind of new

powers the "super regulator" will have, and whether it will be Britain's banking system, particularly after Barings merchant bank collapsed under the weight of derivatives trading losses of $1.3 billion.
could prevent financial disasters. All the regulation in the world cannot stop concerted attempts at fraud, since the industry by its nature depends on taking risk.

"You'll never stop the rogue trader. You can regulate to stop it but there's always a way around it," said a trader at a British bank. "People have a lot of power and can do a lot of damage even within their trading limits."
The main concern for market players was that high-profile cases should not be used as an excuse to impose draconian laws which would stifle the whole industry.

"A few good laws, well-enforced can often do better than an array of regulations," said Jeffrey Golden, a partner specialising in derivatives law at Allen & Overy. "The overall record in derivatives is still exceptionally good. We need to ensure what follows is flexible enough to allow growth."

An organisation with too severe a reputation could be a threat to innovative products and the niche market trading which has helped build London's status as a place where almost anything can be traded.

But market participants were cautiously optimistic the new system will be simpler, particularly for overseas investors who may be blinded by the array of organisations which make up the current regime.

"Bringing everything together makes a lot of sense, but it will depend on what other changes are made at the same time," said Tejit Bath, head of European derivatives at BZW in London. "It will take time to see the impact."

Belchambers said while there were big pluses to the plans, there were also concerns that the SIB will be less approachable to industry groups, which will feel less able to go to the regulator with their worries.
Indeed the size of the new SIB is a major concern for many in the industry.
"The Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) was always very willing to learn, and was very approachable," said a senior salesman at a Japanese house in London.
"A huge unwieldy organisation could have worse internal communications, and be less likely to stop trouble."

David Andrews, a director of the European credit rating agency IBCA said the system would not be any more successful, and there would be unnecessary duplication of effort as the BoE would have to remain the lender of last resort.
"In the U.S. where the Securities Exchange Commission is in charge, divisions within the organisation are a real problem," he said.
